sections.body: An essay has an INTRODUCTION (hook + thesis: your main claim), BODY paragraphs (one point each, with evidence and explanation) and a CONCLUSION (sum up, don't add new points).
A useful body paragraph pattern is PEE: Point, Evidence, Explanation.
Argument essays also answer the strongest counter-argument. This makes your case more convincing, not less.

options: The essay's main claim, usually in the introduction
The last sentence of every paragraph
hints: It tells the reader what you'll argue.
'School uniforms should be optional because they limit self-expression' is one. What job does it do?
quiz.explain: A thesis statement is your main claim, set out in the introduction.

quiz.q: Why address a counter-argument in an argument essay?
options: It shows you've considered other views and strengthens your case
hints: Answering them makes you more convincing.
A lawyer who prepares for the other side's points usually does better. Why?
quiz.explain: Answering the strongest objection shows fairness and makes your argument more convincing.

quiz.q: In the PEE pattern for a body paragraph, what is the job of the Explanation?
options: To show how the evidence supports your point
To introduce a new point for the next paragraph
To repeat the quotation word for word
hints: PEE is Point, Evidence, Explanation. What's left to do after giving evidence?
Evidence on its own doesn't argue anything. Something has to link it back to the point.
In a science report, the Results section gives the data and the Discussion says what that data means for the hypothesis. Which part of PEE is like the Discussion?
quiz.explain: The Explanation links the evidence back to your point, showing the reader why it proves what you claim.
